issues.description: HAS_NUMERIC pre-filter is asymptotically wrong: numbers like 100/200/etc. appear inside many non-numeric font weights via shorthand values, but the bigger hole is omitting the 'normal'/'bold' synonyms in primary='named-where-possible' shortcut.
issues.detail: The regex matches only the nine numeric codes. That is correct as a 'has any numeric weight' probe, but the matching set in NUMERIC_TO_NAMED is the union of relative+non-numeric *targets*, not the full named space. The author should state the invariant: 'fast-path skips iff value cannot possibly trigger a report under primary'. Worth a comment proving each pre-filter is a safe over-approximation.

issues.description: HAS_PERCENTAGE regex is built from PERCENTAGE_SELECTORS without escaping the '%' sign, and lacks the case-insensitive flag that HAS_KEYWORD has; inconsistency between sibling invariants.
issues.detail: PERCENTAGE_SELECTORS presumably contains tokens like '0%','100%'. '%' is regex-safe, but the anchor '(?:^|[,\s])' silently fails when selectors are separated by other whitespace forms (tabs are \s, fine; but no flag mismatch with HAS_KEYWORD's /i). State the invariant once and apply it symmetrically across both regexes.

issues.description: Performance claim is asserted without measurement evidence in the PR description.
issues.detail: The change is plausibly faster (skipping parseSelector / valueParser on values that cannot trigger), but no benchmark numbers, no profiler output, no before/after timing on a representative corpus is included. 'Premature optimization is the root of all evil — yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%.' Show that this is the 3%.

issues.description: Each pre-filter regex deserves a one-line literate comment stating the safety invariant.
issues.detail: For a reader six months from now, '/:not\(/i' as the walkRules filter is obvious; '/:/' on selector-pseudo-element-colon-notation is less so (it includes attribute selectors, pseudo-classes, namespaces). A single comment per filter — 'safe over-approximation: any selector that could report must match' — would make these correct-by-inspection rather than correct-by-trust.

issues.description: import-notation fast-path uses /url\(/i but the rule's reporting logic is presumably based on parsed value-parser nodes; the two notions of 'contains url()' should be proven equivalent.
issues.detail: A params string like '\"url(x)\"' (literal inside a string) matches the regex but is a string-form import, not a url() form. State and verify the invariant that any params reportable under primary='string' contains an unquoted 'url(' token, and that any reportable under primary='url' does not.

issues.description: media-feature-range-notation context regex '(?:min|max)-' is broader than intended and could match within identifiers.
issues.detail: 'min-' / 'max-' as a substring will match e.g. a custom media query named '--my-min-thing' or feature tokens that merely contain the substring. As a *fast-path filter* this is still a safe over-approximation (false positives only cost us the slow path), so it is sound — but worth a comment naming it as such so a future reader doesn't 'tighten' it into incorrectness.

review.summary: The PR is a sensible set of fast-path filters that short-circuit expensive parsing (valueParser, parseSelector) when the input cannot possibly produce a report. The optimizations are mostly UNDER-AUDITED rather than wrong: each filter is implicitly claiming 'any value that would trigger the rule passes this regex,' but that safety invariant is never stated in code or in the PR description. NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT applies to nearly every filter. The performance claim itself is asserted without a measurement — no profile, no before/after numbers on a representative corpus — so this is exactly the case where the motto applies: probably in the critical 3%, but show your work. No asymptotic errors found; the data-structure choice (Map + RegExp from the same token set) is appropriate.
